questions.title: gRPC streaming modes
questions.description: In gRPC, which streaming mode lets both the client and server send a stream of messages independently over a single call?
questions.explanation: Bidirectional streaming opens one call in which both sides read and write message streams independently, unlike server- or client-streaming which stream in only one direction.

options.text: Client streaming
Unary
Server streaming
Bidirectional streaming

questions.title: Protobuf vs JSON wire format
questions.description: What is the main wire-format advantage of Protocol Buffers over JSON for service-to-service communication?
questions.explanation: Protobuf serializes to a compact binary form using field numbers instead of repeated text keys, yielding smaller payloads and faster parse/serialize than text JSON.

options.text: It guarantees exactly-once delivery
It requires no schema definition to decode
Compact binary encoding with smaller payloads and faster parsing
It is human-readable in a browser without tooling

questions.title: Lambda vs Kappa system-design
questions.description: What distinguishes the Kappa system-design from the Lambda system-design for data processing?
questions.explanation: Kappa drops Lambda's separate batch layer and treats everything as a single stream-processing pipeline, reprocessing history by replaying the log instead of maintaining duplicated batch and speed code paths.

options.text: Kappa requires strong consistency across all nodes
Kappa processes only bounded batch data and never streams
Kappa uses a single stream pipeline and replays the log, with no separate batch layer
Kappa adds a third serving layer on top of batch and speed layers

questions.title: Tumbling vs sliding windows
questions.description: In stream processing, how does a tumbling window differ from a sliding window?
questions.explanation: Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping, so each event belongs to exactly one window; sliding windows overlap and can include an event in multiple windows.

options.text: Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping; sliding windows overlap
Tumbling windows grow without bound; sliding windows are fixed
Sliding windows can only be used for batch jobs
Tumbling windows are defined by gaps of inactivity

questions.title: Session windows
questions.description: What defines the boundary of a session window in stream processing?
questions.explanation: A session window groups events separated by less than a configured gap of inactivity; the window closes once no events arrive for the gap duration, so its length is data-driven.

options.text: A gap of inactivity longer than a configured timeout
A fixed number of events regardless of time
The arrival of a watermark message
A fixed clock interval like every 60 seconds

questions.title: Watermarks for late events
questions.description: What role does a watermark play in an event-time stream processor?
questions.explanation: A watermark is the processor's assertion that no events with a timestamp earlier than it should still arrive, letting it close windows and emit results while deciding how to handle stragglers that arrive afterward.

options.text: It encrypts each event with a unique signature
It forces all events to be processed in strict arrival order
It marks how far event time has progressed so windows can close despite out-of-order data
It deduplicates events by content hash

questions.title: Exactly-once stream processing
questions.description: How do stream processors like Flink achieve exactly-once processing semantics across failures?
questions.explanation: They take periodic consistent checkpoints (distributed snapshots) of operator state and input offsets, so on failure they roll back to the last checkpoint and replay, making the effect of each record applied exactly once.

options.text: By processing each record on every node simultaneously
Periodic consistent checkpoints of state plus offset rollback and replay
By disabling all retries so nothing is processed twice
By requiring the network to never drop packets

questions.title: HyperLogLog cardinality
questions.description: What problem does the HyperLogLog data structure solve efficiently?
questions.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements (cardinality) in a huge stream using a tiny fixed amount of memory, trading a small error rate for not storing every element.

options.text: Finding the most frequent element exactly
Storing the exact set of all elements seen
Approximating the count of distinct elements using very little memory
Sorting a stream of numbers in place

questions.title: Count-min sketch
questions.description: What does a count-min sketch approximate, and what is its characteristic error direction?
questions.explanation: A count-min sketch estimates the frequency of items in a stream using hashed counters; because of hash collisions it can overcount but never undercount, so its estimates are upper bounds.

options.text: Distinct element count, always exactly
Item frequencies, with estimates that may overcount but never undercount
Item frequencies that may undercount but never overcount
The median of a numeric stream

questions.title: Rendezvous (HRW) hashing
questions.description: How does rendezvous (highest-random-weight) hashing decide which node owns a key?
questions.explanation: Rendezvous hashing computes a hash weight of (key, node) for every node and picks the node with the highest weight, giving consistent-hashing-like minimal remapping without a hash ring or virtual nodes.

options.text: It stores a central table mapping every key to a node
It always assigns the key to the node with the lowest IP address
It round-robins keys across nodes in insertion order
It hashes (key, node) for each node and picks the highest-weight node

questions.title: Redlock distributed lock critique
questions.description: What is a central critique of using Redlock for distributed mutual exclusion in correctness-critical systems?
questions.explanation: Redlock relies on bounded clocks and timing assumptions; GC pauses or clock drift can let a client believe it still holds an expired lock, so it is unsafe without a fencing token to reject stale holders.

options.text: It blocks all reads on the locked resource
Timing/GC pauses can let an expired lock holder still act unless fencing tokens are used
It cannot be implemented on more than one Redis node
It requires a relational database to store the lock

questions.title: Fencing tokens
questions.description: Why does a distributed lock service hand out a monotonically increasing fencing token with each lock grant?
questions.explanation: The protected resource can reject any write carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen, so a delayed or paused old lock holder cannot corrupt state even if it still thinks it owns the lock.

options.text: So the lock never needs to expire
So clients can decrypt the lock contents
So the lock can be shared by multiple holders at once
So the resource can reject writes from a stale, previously-paused lock holder

questions.title: Lease-based locking
questions.description: What is the defining property of a lease compared to a plain lock?
questions.explanation: A lease is a lock with a built-in expiry: if the holder crashes or is partitioned, the lease lapses automatically so the resource is not held forever, at the cost of timing assumptions.

options.text: It guarantees the holder unlimited renewals with no expiry
It is stored only in the client's memory
It automatically expires after a time bound so a crashed holder does not block others forever
It can never be revoked once granted

questions.title: Leveled vs size-tiered compaction
questions.description: Compared to size-tiered compaction, what does leveled compaction in an LSM store optimize for?
questions.explanation: Leveled compaction keeps non-overlapping SSTables per level so a key lives in at most one SSTable per level, bounding read amplification and space overhead at the cost of more write amplification than size-tiered.

options.text: Removing all background I/O entirely
Lower write amplification at the cost of unbounded reads
Lower read and space amplification, trading higher write amplification
Eliminating the need for a write-ahead log

questions.title: Local vs global secondary indexes
questions.description: In a partitioned datastore, what is the trade-off of a local secondary index versus a global one?
questions.explanation: A local (document-partitioned) index lives with each partition's data, so writes are cheap but queries must scatter-gather across all partitions; a global (term-partitioned) index is partitioned by the indexed value, making reads targeted but writes cross-partition.

options.text: Global indexes are always faster for both reads and writes
There is no difference once the data is sharded
Local indexes require a two-phase commit on every read
Local indexes make writes cheap but reads scatter-gather; global indexes make reads targeted but writes cross-partition

questions.title: Wide-column data modeling
questions.description: When modeling data for a wide-column store like Cassandra, what should primarily drive your table and primary-key design?
questions.explanation: Wide-column stores are query-driven: you design one table (and its partition/clustering keys) per access pattern so each query hits a single partition, even if that means denormalizing and duplicating data.

options.text: Foreign-key relationships enforced by the database
The read query patterns, designing a table per access pattern around the partition key
Minimizing the number of tables regardless of queries
Third-normal-form normalization to avoid any duplication

questions.title: Capacity planning headroom
questions.description: Why do teams provision capacity well above measured average load rather than near peak utilization?
questions.explanation: Headroom absorbs traffic spikes, instance failures, deploys, and autoscaler lag; running near saturation leaves no buffer, so latency degrades sharply once a queue forms at high utilization.

options.text: Because cloud providers bill less for idle capacity
To absorb spikes, failures, and autoscaler lag before latency degrades
Because higher utilization always lowers tail latency
To guarantee exactly-once message delivery

questions.title: Forward-fix vs revert rollback
questions.description: When is a forward-fix (roll forward) preferable to reverting a deployment after a bad release?
questions.explanation: A forward-fix is preferred when a revert is unsafe or impossible — for example after an irreversible schema migration or data change — so you patch forward rather than try to undo state the old code can't read.

options.text: When you want the fastest possible return to the prior known-good state
Only when there is no monitoring in place
When a revert is unsafe, such as after an irreversible schema or data migration
Whenever the bug is trivial and the old version is healthy

questions.title: Load shedding under overload
questions.description: What is the goal of load shedding when a service is overloaded?
questions.explanation: Load shedding deliberately rejects or drops a portion of requests early so the service stays responsive for the rest, preventing a total collapse where every request times out under saturation.

options.text: Buffer all excess requests indefinitely in memory
Reject some requests early so the system stays healthy for the remaining ones
Permanently scale down the service to save cost
Retry every failed request immediately to clear the backlog

questions.title: Connection draining on shutdown
questions.description: What does connection draining accomplish during a graceful shutdown or deploy?
questions.explanation: Draining stops sending new requests to an instance while letting in-flight requests finish before it terminates, so a rolling deploy or scale-in doesn't abruptly kill active connections.

options.text: It lets in-flight requests finish while no new requests are routed to the instance
It flushes the database write-ahead log to disk
It immediately kills all open sockets to free resources fast
It encrypts connections before closing them

questions.title: Multi-region failover orchestration
questions.description: When failing over from a primary region to a standby, what risk does an automated failover specifically need to guard against?
questions.explanation: Automated failover can cause split-brain if the old primary is only partitioned (not dead) and keeps taking writes; orchestration must fence the old primary or require quorum before promoting the standby.

options.text: Split-brain, where a merely-partitioned old primary keeps accepting writes alongside the new one
DNS records propagating too quickly to clients
Read replicas falling out of the load balancer pool
The standby region having more capacity than needed

questions.title: Idempotent leader fencing
questions.description: After a leader election, why might the new leader still need fencing even though the old leader 'lost' the election?
questions.explanation: The deposed leader may be in a long GC or network pause and not yet know it lost; without fencing tokens or epoch numbers, its delayed writes can still reach shared state and corrupt it.

options.text: A paused old leader may not yet know it lost and could still issue stale writes
The new leader has no network connectivity
The election protocol cannot count votes correctly
Followers refuse to acknowledge any new leader

questions.title: Bcrypt for password storage
questions.description: Why are passwords stored with an adaptive hash like bcrypt instead of a fast hash like SHA-256?
questions.explanation: Bcrypt is deliberately slow and has a tunable work factor plus a built-in salt, making large-scale brute-force and precomputed-table attacks far more expensive than with a fast general-purpose hash.

options.text: It produces shorter output that saves database space
It avoids the need to store any salt
It is reversible so the original password can be recovered
It is deliberately slow with a tunable cost, raising brute-force expense

questions.title: Salting password hashes
questions.description: What attack does adding a unique per-user salt to password hashes primarily defeat?
questions.explanation: A unique salt makes each hash distinct even for identical passwords, defeating precomputed rainbow-table lookups and preventing one cracked hash from revealing every user who shares that password.

options.text: SQL injection against the login form
Man-in-the-middle interception in transit
Cross-site scripting in the browser
Precomputed rainbow-table lookups and shared-password correlation

questions.title: WebSocket connection scaling
questions.description: Why are long-lived WebSocket connections harder to scale behind a stateless load balancer than short HTTP requests?
questions.explanation: Each WebSocket pins an open connection to one server for its lifetime, so load can't be rebalanced per request; capacity is bound by concurrent connections per node and reconnect storms after a deploy can overload the fleet.

options.text: They are limited to one connection per server globally
WebSockets cannot pass through a load balancer at all
They require a new TCP handshake for every message
Each connection is pinned to one server for its lifetime, so load can't rebalance per request

questions.title: Presigned URLs for uploads
questions.description: Why do services hand clients a presigned URL to upload large files directly to object storage?
questions.explanation: A presigned URL lets the client upload straight to the object store with time-limited, scoped credentials, so the application server never proxies the bytes — saving bandwidth and avoiding it as a throughput bottleneck.

options.text: So the object store can validate the file's business logic
So the client uploads directly to storage without the app server proxying the bytes
So the upload bypasses all authentication
So the file is automatically compressed in transit

questions.title: Resumable / chunked uploads
questions.description: What is the main benefit of chunked, resumable uploads for very large files over unreliable networks?
questions.explanation: Splitting the file into chunks means a dropped connection only requires re-sending the failed chunk rather than restarting the entire upload, and chunks can be uploaded in parallel.

options.text: It compresses the file to a single block
It removes the need to authenticate the upload
A failure only re-sends the affected chunk instead of restarting the whole upload
It guarantees the file is virus-free

questions.title: Read amplification
questions.description: What does 'read amplification' mean in a storage engine?
questions.explanation: Read amplification is the ratio of physical reads performed to satisfy one logical read; in LSM trees a single key lookup may probe multiple SSTables across levels, amplifying the I/O work.

options.text: Reads getting faster as the dataset grows
One logical read triggering multiple physical reads across data structures
Duplicating every read to a replica for safety
Caching all reads in memory permanently

questions.title: Space amplification
questions.description: What is space amplification in a database storage engine?
questions.explanation: Space amplification is the ratio of on-disk bytes used to the logical size of live data; obsolete versions, tombstones, and pending compaction can make the store occupy more disk than the live dataset requires.

options.text: Indexing the same column twice
Compressing data to use less disk than its logical size
Using more disk than the logical data size due to stale versions and pending compaction
Replicating data to additional nodes

questions.title: Serializable isolation
questions.description: What does the serializable isolation level guarantee?
questions.explanation: Serializable guarantees that concurrent transactions produce a result equivalent to some serial (one-at-a-time) ordering, preventing all anomalies including write skew, at the cost of more contention or aborts.

options.text: Concurrent transactions behave as if run one at a time in some order
Reads never block under any circumstance
Transactions are guaranteed to never abort
Only dirty reads are prevented

questions.title: Phantom reads
questions.description: What is a phantom read in transaction isolation?
questions.explanation: A phantom read occurs when a transaction re-runs a range query and sees new rows that another committed transaction inserted matching the predicate, even though existing rows it already read are unchanged.

options.text: The same row returning two different values in one read
A deadlock between two writers
A re-run range query returns new rows inserted by another committed transaction
Reading a value that was never committed

questions.title: MVCC concurrency
questions.description: How does multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) let readers avoid blocking on writers?
questions.explanation: MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row tagged by transaction timestamp, so a reader sees a consistent snapshot from its start time while writers create new versions, removing read-write locking contention.

options.text: Each table is limited to a single concurrent transaction
All rows are locked for the duration of any transaction
Readers see a consistent snapshot of older row versions while writers create new versions
Writers are forced to wait until all readers finish

questions.title: Deadlock handling in databases
questions.description: How do most relational databases typically resolve a deadlock between two transactions?
questions.explanation: The database detects the cycle in its wait-for graph and aborts one transaction (the victim), rolling it back so the other can proceed; the application is expected to retry the aborted one.

options.text: Detect the wait cycle and abort one transaction as the victim, expecting a retry
Pause both transactions forever until an admin intervenes
Silently commit both with partial results
Merge the two transactions into one

questions.title: Two-phase locking
questions.description: What is the defining rule of two-phase locking (2PL)?
questions.explanation: In 2PL a transaction acquires all the locks it needs in a growing phase and releases them in a shrinking phase, never acquiring a new lock after releasing any — which is what guarantees serializability.

options.text: Every transaction must use two separate connections
Locks are held for exactly two seconds each
Locks may be acquired and released in any interleaved order
A transaction never acquires a new lock after it has released any lock

questions.title: Inverted index for search
questions.description: What is the core data structure behind a full-text search engine, and what does it map?
questions.explanation: An inverted index maps each term (token) to the list of documents (and positions) containing it, so a search resolves by looking up posting lists rather than scanning every document.

options.text: A hash of each document's contents
A B-tree mapping document IDs to their full text
A queue of pending search requests
An inverted index mapping each term to the documents that contain it

questions.title: Edge computing benefit
questions.description: What is the primary benefit of running compute at edge locations close to users rather than only in a central region?
questions.explanation: Executing logic at the edge cuts the round-trip distance to the user, reducing latency and origin load for tasks like personalization, auth checks, or caching close to the request.

options.text: Removing the need for TLS encryption
Guaranteeing strong global consistency
Eliminating the need for any central data store
Lower latency by processing requests near the user

questions.title: Cold start in serverless
questions.description: What causes a 'cold start' latency spike in serverless functions?
questions.explanation: When no warm instance is available, the platform must provision a container and initialize the runtime and code before handling the request, adding startup latency that warm invocations avoid.

options.text: The function ran out of disk space
The function's database is being migrated
The platform must spin up and initialize a new runtime before serving the request
The CDN cache has been purged

questions.title: Modulo vs consistent hashing for cache
questions.description: Why is consistent hashing preferred over a simple hash(key) % N for routing keys to a cache cluster?
questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, changing the node count N remaps almost every key, causing a mass cache miss; consistent hashing remaps only the keys near the added or removed node, preserving most of the cache.

options.text: Adding or removing a node remaps only a small fraction of keys instead of nearly all
It makes every lookup O(1) with no hashing
It guarantees every node holds exactly the same keys
It eliminates the need for cache expiration

questions.title: Hot key problem in caching
questions.description: What is the 'hot key' problem in a sharded cache, and a common mitigation?
questions.explanation: A single extremely popular key concentrates all its traffic on one shard, overloading it; mitigations include replicating that key across nodes or adding a small local in-process cache for it.

options.text: One very popular key overloads its shard; mitigate by replicating or locally caching it
Too many keys exist; mitigate by deleting old ones
Keys are too large; mitigate by sharding each key's bytes
Keys expire too quickly; mitigate by disabling TTLs

questions.title: Geo-DNS routing
questions.description: How does geo-DNS (latency- or geography-based DNS routing) direct users to the nearest data center?
questions.explanation: The authoritative DNS server returns different IP addresses based on the resolver's location or measured latency, steering each user toward the closest or fastest region at name-resolution time.

options.text: It returns region-specific IPs based on the resolver's location or latency
It load-balances by rewriting the HTTP request body
It encrypts the DNS response per user
It caches the user's session in DNS

questions.title: Anycast routing
questions.description: What does anycast accomplish when the same IP address is advertised from many locations?
questions.explanation: With anycast, multiple sites announce the same IP and BGP routes each client to the topologically nearest one, providing low-latency edge entry and automatic failover when a site withdraws its route.

options.text: Routing each client to the nearest site advertising that IP, with automatic failover
Encrypting all traffic at the network layer
Assigning a unique IP to every user
Broadcasting each packet to every site simultaneously

questions.title: Distributed global rate limiting
questions.description: Why is enforcing a global rate limit across many API server instances harder than on a single server?
questions.explanation: Each instance only sees its own traffic, so a correct global limit needs shared state (e.g., a central Redis counter) or coordination; otherwise N instances each allowing the limit lets through N times the intended rate.

options.text: Instances see only their own traffic, so a shared counter or coordination is needed for a true global limit
The load balancer always enforces it automatically
Each instance must store the entire request history forever
Rate limiting cannot be done in software at all

questions.title: Single-flight cache regeneration
questions.description: Beyond probabilistic early recomputation, what locking technique prevents many requests from recomputing the same expired cache entry at once?
questions.explanation: A request-coalescing or single-flight lock lets only the first request recompute the value while others wait for and reuse its result, so an expired hot key is regenerated once instead of by every concurrent caller.

options.text: Disabling the cache entirely during recomputation
Sharding the key across more nodes
A single-flight / request-coalescing lock so only one caller recomputes and others reuse the result
Increasing the database connection pool to infinity

questions.title: Saga vs two-phase commit
questions.description: Why might a microservices system choose a saga over a distributed two-phase commit for a multi-service transaction?
questions.explanation: 2PC holds locks and blocks while waiting on a coordinator, hurting availability across services; a saga uses local transactions plus compensating actions, trading atomicity for availability and looser coupling.

options.text: Sagas eliminate the need for any rollback logic
Sagas require a single shared database
Sagas avoid 2PC's blocking locks by using local commits plus compensating actions
Sagas provide stronger ACID atomicity than 2PC

questions.title: Backfilling a new feature
questions.description: What is a backfill in the context of rolling out a new column or derived dataset?
questions.explanation: A backfill populates the new field or table for existing historical rows — usually as a throttled batch job — so the feature works for old data, not just records created after deployment.

options.text: Deleting rows that lack the new field
Reverting the schema to its previous version
Caching the new column in memory
A batch job that populates the new field for pre-existing historical rows

questions.title: Shadow / dark traffic testing
questions.description: What is the purpose of shadowing (mirroring) production traffic to a new service version?
questions.explanation: Shadow testing replays real production requests against the new version without returning its responses to users, so you can validate correctness and performance under real load with zero user-facing risk.

options.text: Validate a new version under real traffic without its responses reaching users
Encrypt production traffic for compliance
Serve half of users from the new version
Replace load testing with synthetic data

questions.title: Poison pill message
questions.description: What is a 'poison pill' message in a queue-based system?
questions.explanation: A poison pill is a message that consistently fails processing and, without handling, gets retried forever — blocking the partition or burning resources; a dead-letter queue after a retry limit is the standard remedy.

options.text: A message that repeatedly fails processing and must be routed to a dead-letter queue
A duplicate message detected by an idempotency key
A high-priority message that jumps the queue
A message that shuts down the consumer cleanly

questions.title: Dead letter queue purpose
questions.description: What is a dead letter queue (DLQ) used for?
questions.explanation: A DLQ holds messages that could not be processed successfully after retries, isolating them so they don't block the main queue and can be inspected or replayed later.

options.text: To store the highest-priority messages first
To duplicate every message for redundancy
To hold messages that repeatedly fail processing for later inspection
To archive successfully processed messages

questions.title: Graceful shutdown signal
questions.description: On receiving a SIGTERM during a rolling deploy, what should a well-behaved service do before exiting?
questions.explanation: It should stop accepting new work, finish or hand off in-flight requests, flush buffers, and close resources cleanly within the grace period, rather than exiting immediately and dropping active requests.

options.text: Ignore the signal and keep running indefinitely
Stop taking new requests, finish in-flight work, and close resources before exiting
Exit immediately to free the port as fast as possible
Restart itself in place without draining

questions.title: Log compaction in Kafka
questions.description: What does log compaction in a Kafka topic retain?
questions.explanation: Log compaction keeps at least the latest value for each key and removes older superseded values, so the topic can act as a durable changelog/snapshot of the current state per key rather than a full history.

options.text: Only the oldest message per partition
A random sample of messages to save space
Every message forever, just compressed
The most recent value for each key, discarding older superseded ones
